Drugs Lessons from Lisbon

By: John Webb | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
After exposing the growing drug problem in Durban's famed Marine Parade, we travel to Lisbon to see the startling impact of one of the world's most progressive drug policies.

Unique Selling Point:
In the 70's and 80's Portugal was overrun by drug peddlers. Astonishingly, as many as one in 100 Portuguese was addicted to heroin and the scourge became a drain on the country's limited resources. But, thanks to forward-thinking policy makers, the situation has been turned around and the country is respected globally for its rational and humane approach to drug addiction. We'll see first-hand whether the Portuguese approach might provide a blueprint for turning the tide in the drug-trade in places like Durban.

Summary:
Portugal's success in overcoming a significant drug - mostly heroin - problem stems from a change in attitude. Initially, resources were poured into policing the problem as the country followed the global trend in criminalising drug use. But, after little to no success, it was decided to treat drug addiction as a medical rather than a criminal issue. Drug use (not sale) was de-criminalised, and resources diverted to assisting users into overcoming their addictions. The result - while not perfect - has been miraculous. Small wonder then that other countries are looking to Portugal as a blueprint in trying to bring their own drug problems under control.

In a recent Carte Blanche expose on the drug use and criminality currently taking place in the streets behind the famous hotels along the Marine Parade, a city official suggested the drug problem would solve itself once development of the Point area got underway. It appeared a short-sighted approach. Far from solving the issue it would, at best, move it to a different part of the city. In this insert, we'll ask whether the experience of a country like Portugal might provide a more pragmatic and lasting solution.

Press Release:


Drug Lessons from Lisbon
After decades of exposing South Africans’ struggle with drugs and related crime hotspots, Carte Blanche travels to Portugal where a radical policy of decriminalising the use and possession of all drugs has been tested for 18 years and has yielded extraordinary results. With a marked reduction in addiction, overdoses, HIV infection and drug-related crime, we ask could SA take this proven route?
Producer & Presenter: John Webb
Watch the trailer


Script:


Drug Lessons from Lisbon Script.

VO: In the Philippines in southeast Asia, the war on drugs has been taken to the extreme.

ITV: Shaun Shelly [04:50:52] drugs are described as an evil and a scourge to society. And so the response to evil is to make it a criminal activity.

VO: There’s a drugs battle happening in South Africa too. Our version, though, is less brazen and less violent but no less controversial.
But the militarised assault on drugs is, according to this man, not only a mistake but based on a dangerous misconception that ignores the real issue.

ITV: Shaun Shelly STRAP [04:49:36] It's more about the socio economic circumstances that people find them in and the way that they're continually marginalized by the way that we respond to drugs, through things like criminalization, through trying to impose a set of moral standards upon people and making an assumption that all people who use drugs are going to be involved in criminal activity and are bad people which is just simply not true.

VO: His name is Shaun Shelly, an international drugs policy activist. A dependent drug-user who resolved his own drug-related issues, his activism has even caught the attention of the United Nations. While his opinions probably aren’t always popular, his experience is much in demand. And while he takes issue with how drugs are usually dealt with, he knows a crisis when he sees one.

ITV: Shaun Shelly STRAP “Drugs Policy Activist“ [04:49:36] We can‘t tell you exactly how many people in South Africa are using drugs but there's an estimate out of about 75000 injecting drug users. That's probably a bit conservative and certainly we're seeing an increase in the use of drugs in South Africa.

VO: That shouldn’t come as a surprise to regular viewers of Carte Blanche. Over the years we’ve plumbed the depths of addiction and been close-quarter witnesses to the turmoil it’s capable of.
From darkened corners of Tshwane, where the grip of Nyaope has driven addicts into the potentially deadly sharing of blood…

VO: …to the backstreets of Durban where cheap drugs are drawing the desperate from other parts of the country. In these instances, and others like them, the response of the State, of the police, is generally the promise of another crackdown. A mistake, Shelly says.

ITV: Shaun Shelly [05:04:59] if you arrest a young person for drug possession, unrelated to any other factors in their life, they are seven to eight times more likely to be arrested in their 40s for a violent crime. They're also two to three times more likely to become drug dependent in their life.

Link (Video Diary) According to Shelly, we’re dealing with a policy crisis. If that’s true, what - if anything - can be done to fix it. Finding a possible answer means a packed bag and a trip abroad.

VO: That’s because in several countries a truce has been declared in the war on drugs… well, at least with some of the combatants.

VO: The man with his back to the camera we’ll call Paulo. It’s not his real name and, in the next ___ seconds, you won’t see his face. That’s because he’s a drug user. Something he’s not particularly proud of.

VO: He’s been caught on the streets with a small amount of cocaine, but this isn’t an interrogation and the people opposite him aren’t detectives. They’re health professionals - part of a team of doctors, psychologists and social workers.

VO: These are the offices of what’s known as the Commission for the Dissuasion of Drug Abuse or CDT in Lisbon, Portugal. Now a tourism mecca, friendly and with a textured history, Lisbon hasn’t always been as peaceful as it appears today.

LINK: It’s one of Europe’s grittier capitals: by no means seedy, but you can sense that this city has been through some rough times. From earthquakes, to conquest and economic collapse – it’s pretty much seen it all. But, in the 80s and 90’s it faced a challenge that threatened the very fabric of society.

VO: Shortly after a revolution ended 40 years of dictatorship, there was a drugs explosion in Portugal. By the late 1980’s an estimated 100 thousand people were addicted to heroin – about one percent of the population. Other substances flourished, too, and it’s said that - at the time – everyone knew someone on drugs.

ITV: Joao Goulao [00:59:54] I was twenty when our revolution happened and shortly after I had some friends, some experiences with cannabis for instance, problems. And I remember from the group of students with whom I used to have this, we were ten close friends, five of them died from drug related problems. (CUT) it was really devastating our society.

VO: Like many in Portugal, Dr.Joao Goulao carries a personal burden from Portugal’s drugs epidemic, and it’s left him with an unusual take on their impact.

ITV: Dr João Goulão – Strap “National Drugs Co-ordinator, Portugal.” [00:36:32 – towards end] So instead of saying, okay the drugs are bad, my approach to my daughter, 14 years old, is people will tell you that drugs are bad, dangerous. No, no drugs are good. They are so good, that they are dangerous because they are so good that they may become the centre of your life.

VO: If it sounds eccentric, consider this: Goulao is one of the architects of what is arguably the most effective drugs policy in the world. Adopted in 2001, it’s seen severe addiction rates plummet – falling by more than 50 percent in the first ten years. Its drug-induced death rate is five times lower than the European average. Go in search, and you’ll find signs of the policy in action:

VO: Here, users queue for clean needles. It’s a van operated by an NGO in partnership with the State. Those wanting to give up heroin are given methadone pills as a replacement. Two of these vans service hundreds of people across Lisbon each day – beneficiaries of a policy that has decriminalised drugs for personal consumption. From cannabis to heroin and everything in between.

LINK: It’s a policy that has won Portugal admirers - and a few critics – around the world. At its centre is this principle: that you treat drug addiction and drug use as a medical issue rather than a criminal one.

VO: Drugs are still illegal in Portugal, but the change in approach means anyone caught using small, predetermined quantities won’t end up in court and possibly jail. For drug traffickers and pushers prison awaits; they’re still pursued by the police and the courts. Drug users are looked after by the country’s Health Department.

ITV: Joao Goulao [00:36:32]This is a disease like the others with the same dignity as the others and people suffer from it deserve the same dignity as other patients, people. There are other chronic relapsing diseases self-inflicted let's say for instance, some sorts of diabetes, that depend on what you eat. Okay, but we do not criminalise someone because it's too much sugar.

ITV: Nuno Capaz [22:41:04.17] because it is considered an administrative offence, legally it's very similar to being caught driving without the seatbelt. So, it’s like in those situations where the person is caught driving without his seatbelt because it is an administrative offence, the person is not arrested, he doesn't get a criminal record out of that.

VO: Dr Nuno Capaz heads up Lisbon’s Drug Dissuasion Centre. It’s his job to help ensure good policy becomes good practise.

ITV: Nuno Capaz – STRAP “VP: Commission for Dissuasion of Drug Addiction” [22:38:26.11] Our background is health, so our concern is health issues. So, if we see someone that might be in some sort of problem or trouble, we try to help. It's as simple as that. We do have the law that we have to apply. We might eventually have to decide upon some sanctions but never the less everything is health-centred so there is a lot of compassion involved in all the procedure.

VO: And that’s good news for “Paulo”. The system has spared him a criminal record and, instead, Capaz and his team are sending him for counselling.

ITV: Nuno Capaz [22:44:25.23] At some point he just said well if people are willing to help me, I might as well accept it and that doesn't mean he is going to stop using all together eventually but at least it shows that he is in tune with having a more responsible and more conscious relation with the substance that they are using and that is basically our goal.

VO: Given the policy’s success, it’s small wonder that last year alone 50 international delegations visited Portugal to take a look for themselves.
Link: So, does the Portuguese example provide a blueprint for how things should be done in South Africa? Well, for starters the two countries have two very different health care systems. But perhaps there is a lesson to be had in how the Portuguese have approached this challenge. And that can be summarised in one word: compassion.

VO: It’s probably not a word you’d generally associate with South Africa’s current policy, and the fallout from that is seen on the streets of places like Durban.
John Webb Question: Can this be used as a blueprint?

ITV Nunu Capaz [22:54:20.17] decriminalizing it is copyable everywhere in the world (CUT) when you get to the sanctions part, you remove the criminal sanctions. You leave the financial fines, you leave the community service (CUT) but you remove the jail sentence, you remove the criminal record and that's decriminilising. That is copyable everywhere in the world. It will not bring results, extraordinary results right away but at least it will reduce the stigma associated with drug users.

ITV: Shaun Shelly [05:00:02] we've been so brainwashed and so led to believe that you know that free availability of drugs will cause chaos, unless we actually see it for own eyes it's difficult to believe. No matter what the data is, you need to see the stories, you need to understand the impacts of people and the direct impact on their lives.
ENDS.

VO: It’s probably not a word you’d generally associate with South Africa’s current policy, and the fallout from that is seen on the streets of places like Durban. John Webb Question: Can this be used as a blueprint? ITV Nunu Capaz [22:54:20.17] decriminalizing it is copyable everywhere in the world (CUT) when you get to the sanctions part, you remove the criminal sanctions. You leave the financial fines, you leave the community service (CUT) but you remove the jail sentence, you remove the criminal record and that's decriminilising. That is copyable everywhere in the world. It will not bring results, extraordinary results right away but at least it will reduce the stigma associated with drug users. ITV: Shaun Shelly [05:00:02] we've been so brainwashed and so led to believe that you know that free availability of drugs will cause chaos, unless we actually see it for own eyes it's difficult to believe. No matter what the data is, you need to see the stories, you need to understand the impacts of people and the direct impact on their lives. ENDS.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): After exposing the growing drug problem in Durban's famed Marine Parade, we travel to Lisbon to see the startling impact of one of the world's most progressive drug policies.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: In the 70's and 80's Portugal was overrun by drug peddlers. Astonishingly, as many as one in 100 Portuguese was addicted to heroin and the scourge became a drain on the country's limited resources. But, thanks to forward-thinking policy makers, the situation has been turned around and the country is respected globally for its rational and humane approach to drug addiction. We'll see first-hand whether the Portuguese approach might provide a blueprint for turning the tide in the drug-trade in places like Durban.
metadata.Summary: Portugal's success in overcoming a significant drug - mostly heroin - problem stems from a change in attitude. Initially, resources were poured into policing the problem as the country followed the global trend in criminalising drug use. But, after little to no success, it was decided to treat drug addiction as a medical rather than a criminal issue. Drug use (not sale) was de-criminalised, and resources diverted to assisting users into overcoming their addictions. The result - while not perfect - has been miraculous. Small wonder then that other countries are looking to Portugal as a blueprint in trying to bring their own drug problems under control. In a recent Carte Blanche expose on the drug use and criminality currently taking place in the streets behind the famous hotels along the Marine Parade, a city official suggested the drug problem would solve itself once development of the Point area got underway. It appeared a short-sighted approach. Far from solving the issue it would, at best, move it to a different part of the city. In this insert, we'll ask whether the experience of a country like Portugal might provide a more pragmatic and lasting solution.
